analysis of the overall trend of budget allocation for the Health Sector before furnishing its
replies to the Committee and desist from skirting the crux of the issue raised by the Committee.

the Health Sector since 2013-14 year-wise in real terms at constant 2011-12 prices after adjusting
for inflation. (para 3.6)
The Committee observes that stepping up investments in public healthcare is vital to
sustaining India's economic growth. Though the Government has set a lofty target of raising
77

78
health spending to 2.5% of GDP by the year 2024-25 in the National Health Policy, 2017, the
quantum of provision for public healthcare as laid out in the Union Budget 2017-18 is just 29%

is to be achieved, 1% of it would need to come from the central expenditures. However, the

seen the light of day. The Committee is dismayed with the slow pace of Department in getting
the pre-requisites completed in case of these two projects and strongly recommends that the
progress of these projects may be reviewed at the highest level in the Department with a view
to remove the stumbling blocks. (para 3.34)
LADY HARDING MEDICAL COLLEGE (LHMC)
The Committee would like the Department to pursue implementation of the Redevelopment
Plan of LHMC with a sense of urgency and promptitude as much delay has already taken place.
The Committee would also like to be apprised of the revised project cost and timeline for
execution of the Redevelopment Plan. (para 3.37)
The Committee strongly recommends that the project should not get stuck in administrative
and procedural delays. Efforts should be made to expedite the process of getting approvals on
priority basis. The Committee also recommends that the Department should devise a plan of
action considering the available physical and financial resources and set realistic timeframe for
the completion of project. The Committee would like to be apprised of the progress made in this
regard. (para 3.40)
ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIIMS), NEW DELHI
The Committee is alarmed to note that despite its exhortation in the past, the issue of
manpower shortage in the AIIMS has not been addressed so far and seems to have become
endemic which is a matter of serious concern as it has a direct bearing on the quality of care
at the premier Institute which is a boon for poor patients as it offers them treatment, free of
cost. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the manpower shortage at AIIMS be sorted
out in a time bound manner so that the resources available there could be made full use of. The
Committee also desires to be apprised of the updated status of vacancies across all categories of
posts. (para 3.43)
POSTGRADUATE INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES AND RESEARCH (PGI), CHANDIGARH
The Committee notes that though the Department has inter alia submitted that 'Recruitment
is an ongoing process and the Institute is taking steps to recruit the people on all the vacant
posts' but has not indicated the headway made towards fdling up the vacancies at PGIMER,

84
Chandigarh. The Committee treats the reply unsatisfactory. The Committee, therefore, desires
to be apprised of the achievement in terms of filling up of vacant posts vis-a-vis sanctioned posts
at PGIMER, Chandigarh during the last one year. The Committee also wishes to be apprised
whether the funds allocated for expected filling up of vacancies have been utilized or not during
the year 2017-18. (para 3.47)
REGIONAL INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (RIMS), IMPHAL
Though, the Committee appreciates the Department's effort to have a more transparent
administrative process for procurement of medical equipments and construction activities at the
institute, it seems that the Department has missed the boat on the deliverable required to
expedite the capital projects at the Institute. The Committee observes that the basic pre-requisite
to start an institute is development of infrastructure. The Committee finds the pace of work
extremely slow resulting to cost and time overruns which cannot be overlooked at any cost. The
Committee would like the Department to furnish the reasons for the same. (para 3.54)
NATIONAL ORGAN TRANSPLANT PROGRAMME (NOTP)
The Committee hopes that the evaluation of the NOTP would have been carried out and the
loopholes plugged by now. The Committee desires to be updated in this regard. The Committee
simultaneously observes that the re-evaluation of the Program would not have be necessitated
had it been conceive d empirically during the initial stage itself. (para 3.57)
SERA AND VACCINE MANUFACTURING UNITS
From the information submitted by the Department, the Committee could gather that out
of total requirement of vaccines of BCG, TT,DPT for the years 2014-15 & 2015-16, vaccine
supplied by these vaccine institutes is way less compared to procurement of vaccines from the
open market. The Committee is of the firm view that these vaccines producing institutes at
Kasauli, Coonoor and Chennai should meet most of the vaccine requirement of the country so
that the supplies on account of any unforeseen crisis in private commercial production is not
disrupted and the health security of the citizens is ensured. (para 3.60)
CENTRAL DRUGS STANDARD CONTROL ORGANISATION (CDSCO)
The Committee observes that onus of monitoring drug quality rests primarily with State
Drug regulatory Authorities. However, many State Governments have not modernized their drug
regulatory framework despite the fact that the competence of their drug regulatory infrastructure
is not of the desired level. Hence, it is imperative that the State Drug regulatory apparatus is
upgraded to enable them to perform their assigned functions efficiently and transparently. It is
in this context that the revamping of the existing drug regulatory structure assumes added
significance and needs to be addressed on priority basis. Though the Department in its reply has
stated that the recommendation regarding the strengthening the drug regulatory system has
been noted for compliance, no solid roadmap has been indicated for implementation of the
assurance. The Committee would like to have a detailed status note on the measures proposed
to be taken for improving the drug regulatory system in the country. (para 3.63)

85
FOOD SAFETY AND STANDARD AUTHORITY OF INDIA (FSSAI)
The Department's reply reflects budgetary figures only and does not mention the achievements
of target of FSSAI during the last financial year. Therefore, the Committee would like to be
apprised of the tangible work undertaken by the FSSAI separately in the fields of safety and
regulation of the food items for human consumption against ````` 76.95 crore spent on these two
accounts. The Committee would also like the FSSAI address the lingering issue of time-lag in
utilization of allotted funds. (para 3.66)
The Committee would like to reiterate the importance of the scheme for 'Strengthening of
the Food Testing System" in the country including provision for Mobile Food Testing Labs which
would go a lay way in ensuring the availability of safe food for common people. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that concerted efforts need to be made by the Department to kick-start
the scheme at the earliest with adequate budgetary requirements given the vital importance of
the objective of the Scheme. (para 3.71)
The Committee appreciates the initiative of the Department of Safe Water Portal through
which consumer can view that test reports of water samples based on licence number of FSSAI.
This portal has been amplified as a 'confidence building exercise' for the packaged drinking water
and reaffirms the right of the consumer that the packaged water purchased is safe and of high
quality. The Committee is of the view that a similar portal for all packaged food items can be
designed entailing all information and test reports of the food products so as to educate and
inform the consumer about their quality and safety. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
work in this aspect be expedited. Further, the Committee would like to be apprised about the
details of INFLONET and its objectives. (para 3.74)
NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR PREVENTION AND CONTROL OF CANCER, DIABETES.
CARDIOV ASCULAR DISEASE AND STROKE (NPCDCS)
From the replies given by the Department, the Committee observes that approval for
setting up of 12 State Cancer Institutes and 13 Tertiary Care Centres have been given and the
projects are underway at different stages. The Committee would like to be apprised of the list
of States where these Cancer Centres have been approved and status of these projects at present.
Also, the physical targets and the dedicated timelines for these projects may also be provided.
Secondly, the Committee also wishes to know which States have sent their proposals for establishing
State Cancer Institutes and Tertiary Care Centre and what kind of deficiencies have been
identified by the Centre Government in their proposals. Also, the list of States who have reverted
back with the revised proposals may also be given. The Committee is of the view that the since
cancer is a life threatening disease, it not only takes toll on physical health but shudder the
patient's emotional and financial stability. If cancer treatment is made available to every needy
patient in his nearby areas, it would be easier for them to manage their physical well being. The
Committee is of the opinion that the Department should contemplate to make adequate
modifications in the guidelines for setting up of the SCI/TCCCs in the States. The Department
may also consider the option of public private partnership (PPP) method by allowing the private

86
hospitals to set up their Cancer Care Centres in selected States where there is no cancer
treatment facilities available, thereby providing state of art cancer treatment facilities to the
needy people. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the data on number of people
attending to and getting treatment at SCC/ICCCs in the States since the day these centres are
made operational. (para 3.78)
NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL ORGANISATION (NACO)
METRO BLOOD BANK PROJECT
The Committee notes that the Department has informed that setting up Metro Blood Bank
project was initially proposed in two locations i.e. Delhi and Chennai in phase I with budget
outlay of ````` 404.00 crore to be implemented over 7 years. However, land allocation in Delhi could
not be finalised due to which the matter remained pending with LG and it has been shifted to
Kolkata as West Bengal Government showed keen interest in it. The Committee is constrained
to observe that despite the passage of considerable time since its approval, the project of Metro
Blood Banks is stuck in a limbo since 2014-15. The Committee apprehends that the gains
achieved in managing AIDS may be frittered due to inordinate delay in setting up of four Metro
Blood Banks which has now been scaled down to two. The Committee is equally disappointed that
Metro Blood Banks in Delhi had to be shelved due to bureaucratic red tape which does not auger
well for maintaining the tempo of success achieved so far in managing AIDS epidemic in India.
The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should pull up its socks
and ensure that four Metro Blood Banks are set up within a dedicated time frame, and for this
a strong monitoring mechanism should be put in place to ensure completion of the scheme.
(para 3.81)

REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Government on the recommendations
contained in the One Hundredth Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants (Demand No. 43) of
the Department of Health Research for the year 2017-18.
2. Action Taken Notes (ATNs) have been received from the Government in respect of the
recommendations contained in the 100th Report. They have been categorized as follows:
(i) (Chapter-I) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government
have been accepted by the Committee: 2.4, 3.4, 3.8, 3.21,4.6, 5.6, 6.3, 7.4
Total - 8
(ii) (Chapter-II) Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue
in view of the Government's replies: 2.19, 3.10, 3.11, 3.13, 3.18, 6.4, 8.5
Total - 7
(iii) (Chapter-III) Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Government
have not been accepted by the Committee: 2.1, 2.2, 2.10, 2.11, 2.12, 2.15, 3.6,
3.7, 3.15, 4.7, 5.3, 6.6, 8.3
Total - 13
(iv) (Chapter-IV) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Government
are still awaited:
Total - Nil
3. The details of the ATNs are discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.

2
CHAPTER -I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE
GOVERNMENT HA VE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observation
1.1 The Committee notes that there is a huge, persistent and recurring mismatch between the projected
demand for funds and actual allocation of the schemes/projects of the Department of Health Research.
The Department has informed that it has impacted the implementation of schemes of the DHR by
restricting the sanctioning of new units/labs on priority, providing recurring grants to the ongoing projects
and upgradation of the health research infrastructure of ICMR and pendency of extramural proposals due
to non-availability of budgetary allocation. The Committee is of the view that funds constraint should
not be a hurdle in prioritizing health research and developing new drugs, vaccines and diagnostics.
(Para 2.4)
Action Taken
1.2 Observations of the Hon'ble Committee are noted for compliance.
III. INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation
1.3 The Committee notes that there is a huge difference in the funds allocated for ICMR against its
projected demand in all the five years from 2013-14 to 2017-18. The shortfall of funds have been
massive by any standard and is certain to have an adverse bearing on the implementation of various
intramural and extramural research projects of ICMR . Given the satisfactory track-record of ICMR in
utilising the budgeted funds, the Committee wonders as to what financial yardstick was applied leading
to a substantially reduced allocation of funds in BE 2017-18 vis-a-vis the projected demand. In view
of the dynamic International health research environment and the current and future health challenges
of the country, the role of ICMR is very crucial in generating new knowledge in frontier areas of research
in health and related issues. Taking note of the written submission of the Department that an additional
amount of 
`835.00 crore is required for 2017-18 to meet the needs of the Department in new and
emerging areas of health research as per national priorities, the Committee in the earlier part of this
Report has recommended allocation of the additional amount for the Department. The Committee
simultaneously recommends to the Department to deploy the available resources for cutting edge research
for diseases and translating such research into outcomes for tackling diseases which have been prioritized
at National level by the Department of Health Research. (Para 3.4)
Action Taken
1.4 Department appreciates and is thankful to the Hon'ble Committee for highlighting the shortfall of
funds to ICMR and recommending allocation of more funds to meet the needs of emerging areas of
2

3
Health research. As desired, ICMR would take action for prioritizing the research activities in relation to
national health challenges and translating health research outcome for the benefit of the society. ICMR
will deploy its available resources in cutting edge research in the areas like Cancer Research, Diabetes,
Tuberculosis, Innovation and Translational Research, Vector borne diseases, etc.
Recommendation/Observation
1.5 The Committee observes that despite the fact that India contributes disproportionately to the global
disease burden, health research in India is hamstrung by paucity of relevant data and the Secretary (HR)
admitted that "we need large population based surveys" to do meaningful research. The Committee is
of the view that if we are not able to capture relevant data despite the information technology resources
currently available in India, it is indicative of not only infrastructural weaknesses, but suboptimal use
of IT in data collection also. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to develop a strong
database, the Department should work in close coordination with other science agencies, academia, all
research institutes including privately owned research institutes, laboratories, medical universities, medical
colleges and build a strong technology platform for information sharing and research collaborations.
(Para 3.8)
Action Taken
1.6 Managing big data in healthcare generated through multi-dimensional research is a big challenge.
ICMR has now focused its research in big data analytics and it is also proposed to develop a strategy
for data systems and Research Platforms. Major efforts for this will be made under this platform. ICMR
Policy on research data sharing and access will be initiated with establishing a multidisciplinary/multi-
stakeholder committee for developing, guiding and monitoring implementation of policy. It will be followed
by data system organization, creation of a platform for research, disease specific/thematic digital data
repositories and global availability of ICMR generated data in coming years. The MOU recently signed
with Project ECHO will help in this endeavour. ICMR will also work in coordination with other S&T
agencies, medical colleges, Universities for the same.
ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE
Recommendation/Observation
1.7 The Committee observes that the issuing of guidelines for antibiotics use by ICMR to 20 hospitals
is quite recent. The Committee feels that this issue is a serious one which requires immediate attention
and action. The Committee, therefore, believes that a dedicated action plan on antimicrobial resistance,
including antibiotic resistance needs to be prepared by ICMR on a priority basis. The Committee strongly
recommends for standardization of the protocol for the administration of antibiotics and expects that a
process of sensitizing the medical community about the perils of antibiotic resistance should be taken up
on a national scale by involving medical associations, Industry associations, medical academia, media
and other groups. The Committee is also of the view that aggressive awareness generation programmes
regarding use of antibiotics without a prescription must be taken up to educate people in this regard.
(Para 3.21)

4
Action Taken
1.8 A country specific National Action Plan (NAP) has been prepared by all the agencies collectively
under the leadership of WHO. ICMR is a key stakeholder for research and development under NAP.
1.9 For Standardizing administration of Antimicrobials, the ICMR has organized four Antimicrobial
Stewardship workshops to train doctors from 30 hospitals to rationalize antibiotic prescriptions in tertiary
care hospitals.
IV INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT FOR HEALTH RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation
1.10 The Committee has been given to understand that against the projected outlay 
` `145.00 crore for
2017-18 under the head - Establishment of Network of Laboratories for Managing Epidemics & Natural
Calamities, an allocation of ` 59.00 crore has been made in 2017-18 which is higher than the previous
year's allocation of ` 39.25 crore. The Committee observes that India continues to have epidemics due
to various infectious pathogens and it is imperative to promptly respond to localised outbreaks before
they pose bigger health challenges. It is in this context that building a network of well-equipped viral
diagnostic laboratories is necessary. The Committee recommends that the scheme should not be allowed
to be plagued with under funding and the Department should seek more funds, if needed, at RE stage.
(Para 4.6)
Action Taken
1.11 Requirement of `167.65 crores has been projected for the scheme for the year 2017-18.
V. DEVELOPMENT OF INFRASTRUCTURE FOR PROMOTION OF HEALTH RESEARCH
ESTABLISHMENT OF MULTIDISCIPLINARY RESEARCH UNITS (MRUs) IN GOVERNMENT
MEDICAL COLLEGES
Recommendation/Observation
1.12 Against the projected demand of 
`178.00 crore, the scheme has got `36.00 crore only for 2017-18
and this clearly shows that the fund allocation for MRUs is rather low. MRUs are targeted to promote
and encourage quality medical research and provide assistance to State Government medical colleges
across the country to set up appropriate research facilities and carry out focussed research on non-
communicable diseases. Given the growing burden of non-communicable diseases that often require life-
long management, this scheme is of immense importance. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government should ensure that more resources are allocated to MRUs to give an impetus to medical
research on non-communicable diseases. The Committee also recommends that the MRUs should be
benchmarked with the best institutions in their domain internationally. (Para 5.6)
Action Taken
1.13 A minimum requirement of `145.92 crores has been projected for the year 2017-18 in the proposal
for continuation of the scheme beyond 12th Five Year Plan and upto 2019-20.

5
1.14 Performance of MRUs is being reviewed from time to time by the external experts and guidance
is also provided from the national level on the research activities so that MRUs could emerge as excellent
centres of research in the medical colleges.
VI. ESTABLISHMENT OF MODEL RURAL HEALTH RESEARCH UNITS (MRHRUs) IN THE
STATES
Recommendation/Observation
1.15 The Committee is constrained to note that out of the 15 MRHRUs planned to be established during
the Twelfth Plan period, only 8 MRHRUs have been established which have initiated research activities
and the remaining have either been approved only or are in the pipeline. Evidently, the Department has
lagged behind in achieving the targets set for the 12th Five Year Plan. The Committee would therefore
like the Department to ascertain the exact reasons responsible for non-achievement of the targets and
take corrective measures accordingly so that the intended outcomes are achieved in future and there are
no time and cost overruns due to slippages in implementation of this project. (Para 6.3)
Action Taken
1.16 Against the 12th Plan target to establish 15 MRHRUs, 14 MRHRUs have been approved till date.
All the MRHRUs could not initiate the research activities since the Units were sanctioned in phases
starting from 2013-14 and it took time in the allocation of requisite land by the State Government,
construction of the building, procurement of equipment, recruitment of staff and particularly since it
involved creation of health research infrastructure at the rural level. The implementation of this path
breaking initiative is progressing satisfactorily and outcomes will be visible in the very near future.
VII. DEVELOPMENT OF TOOLS/SUPPORT TO PREVENT OUTBREAK OF EPIDEMICS
1.17 The Committee finds that only ` 46 lakh has been spent out of the total allocation of `2.25 crore
during 2016-17 under the head-Development of Tools/Support to Prevent Outbreak of Epidemics and
expenditure of another `37.00 lakhs is in the pipeline. It is obvious that this project is certain to register
huge savings. The Committee would expect the Department to be more prudent in making their estimates
under this Head and ensure that the funds are fully utilized. (Para 7.4)
Action Taken
1.18 Against the allocation of `2.25 crore in 2016-17, the utilisation upto 31.3.2017 is `1.63 crore, as
follows:
(i) National Institute of Virology, Pune and National Institute of Malaria Research, New Delhi
(`37.00 lakhs) and National Institute of Cholera and Enteric Diseases (NICED), Kolkata
(`8.57 lakhs); (ii) SV Institute of Medical Sciences, Tirupati ( `37.88 lakhs) and King Institute

III. INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation
2.3 The Committee observes that India is the highest TB burden country in the world and the biggest
challenge from healthcare point of view is increase in incidence of multi drug resistant and XDRTB,
especially in the rural areas. Though the Government has rolled out the administration of Bedaquiline,
the first TB drug approval by the USFDA in over 40 years, in six public health hospitals in the country
to specifically treat multi-drug resistant TB, a lot remains to be done to improve multidrug resistant TB
treatment outcomes. The Committee therefore recommends that ICMR should focus its research on multi-
drug resistant TB strains with a view to discovering potent drug combinations combating MDRTB. The
Committee desires to be apprised of the initiatives taken in this regard. (Para 3.10)
Action Taken
ICMR initiative to tackle MDR-TB:
2.4 In a joint initiative with the Department of Biotechnology and Ministry of Health & Family Welfare,
the ICMR is conducting the evaluation of TruenatRif an indigenous molecular diagnostic kit for diagnosis
of MDR-TB. The test is found to be at par with another imported molecular test Gene Xpert which is
currently being used under Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP). The TruenatRif is cost
effective, rapid and can be placed at District Microscopy Centers under RNTCP and will facilitate early
detection of MDR-TB thus preventing transmission and spread of MDR-TB. The kit is currently undergoing
feasibility study under RNTCP which is likely to be completed by August, 2017 and would subsequently
be ready for launch and incorporation under RNTCP.
6

7
2.5 ICMR also plans to initiate therapeutic clinical trials for MDR/XDR TB using regimen containing
new drugs.
2.6 Besides a new molecule Transitmycin has been discovered by National Institute of Research in
Tuberculosis (NIRT) in collaboration with IIT, Madras and Periyar University, which has been found to
be effective in MDR-TB in in-vitro studies. The molecule will be taken forward through series of animal
studies and subsequent human trials for development of the drug for treatment of MDR-TB.
2.7 A landscaping exercise has been completed and new drug leads identified in various national and
international Labs have been identified. These will be taken into pre-clinical and clinical testing in
partnership with industry for new drug development.
TB Elimination Programme:
2.8 ICMR has also initiated efforts to tackle TB in mission mode and have initiated process to establish
a suitable institutional framework to bring together all major national players (with international collaborators)
at one platform to help Revised National Tuberculosis Programme (RNTCP) to achieve TB elimination
by 2025. The framework will also have a strong partnership between Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare and other science agencies, national and international organizations. The vision of the proposed
framework is "To achieve Elimination of TB from India by investing in new tools (drugs, diagnostics,
and vaccines) as well as provide these solutions to the world."
Recommendation/Observation
2.9 The Committee observes that Sickle Cell Anaemia and Thalassemia are endemic in certain areas of
the country, particularly in the tribal areas. Sickle Cell Anaemia and Thalassemia are genetic diseases
and cannot be treated by random medicines. The bone marrow transplant is a cure for Sickle Cell
Anaemia, but very few people are able to get that, both for lack of facilities and prohibitive costs. The
Committee would therefore like the Department to focus its research upon these two diseases with a view
to introducing effective interventions into our healthcare system. (Para 3.11)
Action Taken
2.10 ICMR's National Institute of Immunohematology and National Institute of Research in Tribal Health
(NIRTH), Jabalpur are involved in high quality research in the area of Sikcle Cell Anemia and Thalassemia.
ICMR has developed a test for molecular diagnosis of beta thallassemia. ICMR has also set up a Satellite
Centre for sickle cell anemia at Chanderpur, Maharashtra. These efforts will help in cutting edge research
in both these areas. An inter-ministerial Group has been set up by the Department of Biotechnology
(DBT) with ICMR as partner for management Of Sickle Cell Anemia in the country.
AYUSH-ICMR Collaboration
Recommendation/Observation
2.11 India has a strong foundation and rich heritage of AYUSH systems and provide people options to
avail treatment of their choice. The Committee is of the view that the collaboration of ICMR with
AYUSH is a step in the right direction. Such collaborative efforts will provide documented evidence of

8
the side-effects, contra indications and drug reactions, give credibility to AYUSH systems and also help
in fostering a synergy between the two systems of medicines (i.e. Allopathy and AYUSH). If AYUSH is
to be brought to the global stage, validation of AYUSH drugs is imperative. Therefore, the Committee
recommends to the Department to prepare a framework for validation of classical drugs and according
high priority to AYUSH formulations and facilitating interdisciplinary AYUSH research. The Committee
would like to be apprised of the progress made in this direction. (Para 3.13)
Action Taken
2.12 ICMR is fostering research in area of traditional medicine with the support from its National
Institute of Traditional Medicine (NITM) at Belagavi. It is also planned to leverage traditional knowledge
with an attempt to identify promising research leads for their validation for the public good in collaboration
with Ministry of AYUSH wherein other ICMR institutions will also be involved. For this ICMR has
developed a vision document for leveraging traditional knowledge.
Development of Dengue Vaccine
Recommendation/Observation
2.13 The Committee observes that the introduction of the Sanofi dengue vaccine has safety dimensions
and all caution needs to be exercised to ensure that a situation does not arise where the harm done would
outweigh the benefits therefrom. The Committee also observes that given the high incidences of dengue
in different parts of the country, a definite timeline must be given for the development of dengue vaccine
so that cases of dengue are dealt with properly. The Committee would also like to be apprised about the
expenditure incurred in research for development of dengue vaccine in the last five years.  (Para 3.18)
Action Taken
2.14 ICMR is not directly involved in the development of dengue vaccine and has also not incurred any
expenditure on the same. Presently, the only available vaccine for dengue, globally is Dengvaxia of Sanofi
Pasteur. The vaccine is differentially effective against all four serotypes with least effectiveness for
dengue virus type 2. India lacks cross sectional country wide data on seroprevalence of dengue in the
community. ICMR has, therefore, initiated a study to determine age stratified seroprevalence of dengue
in 15 States of the country. Other related viruses like Chikungunya and JE will also be tested.

achieve key goals of Health Research or to make spectacular break-through in the newly-emerging

Further Recommendation
3.6 The Committee notes from the Department's reply that year to year budgetary allocations

discussions and shortfall in allocations have affected implementation of the five newly launched
schemes in 2013-14. However, on perusal of the expenditure figures, the Committee notes that
the same are below the RE allocations made from 2012-13 to 2016-17, thereby leading to cuts

mechanism should be put in place for proper utilization of allocated funds through effective

Recommendation/Observation
3.7 The Committee observes that the health challenges in India are huge and complex due to its large
population, rapid industrialization, demographic transition, huge maternal and infant mortality and high
burden of diseases like communicable diseases (TB, Malaria, HIV, emerging and re-merging infections),
non-communicable diseases (Cardio-vascular diseases, diabetes, cancer etc). To address the high disease
burden, our national health research agenda needs to be updated constantly and indigenous health
products would need to be developed to combat these challenges.
This is all the more important in view of the fact that the global trade and intellectual property
rights regimes have made it difficult to use health products and processes developed outside due to their
high costs and restrictions placed on producing cost effect generics. (Para 2.10)

III. INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH
Recommendation/Observation
3.17 Currently, health research in the country is primarily carried out by 31 Institutes of ICMR which
was established in 1911 and is one of the oldest medical research bodies in the world. The Committee
observes from the information furnished that in two years i.e. 2015 and 2016, only 1685 research papers
(965 in 2015 and 720 in 2016) have been published by ICMR scientists and 3 patents have been granted
against 45 patents filed. This clearly indicates that the health research output is not up to the mark and
not commensurate with the magnitude and disease burden in India. Given the fact that the country
contributes to a fifth of the world's share of diseases (12th Plan Report) and one of the vital elements
in improving this situation is the need for a relevant research base that would equip policy makers to
take informed health policy decisions, the health research output needs to be augmented substantially to
cater to the health challenges faced. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the ICMR should evolve
mechanisms to boost quality health research output by way of building alliances and partnerships and
create a vibrant ecosystem for the purpose. The Committee is of the view that evolving such frameworks
would lead to granting of more patents which, in turn, would generate the much needed funds for ICMR
and health research. (Para 3.6)
Action Taken
3.18 ICMR has noted the observations of the Hon'ble Committee and as suggested will strive hard in
developing new partnerships for enhancing research output. ICMR has recently signed a MoU with
Project ECHO (Extension for Community Healthcare outcome) at the University of New Mexico Health
Science Centre (UNMHSC) with a mission to de-monopolize knowledge and augment the capacity to
provide best healthcare for the remote and underserved people. MoU has also been signed with IIT to
use best technology for innovation and translational research. MoU with AYUSH will help in better
understanding of the Traditional Medicines. More such partnerships will be developed.
Further Recommendation
3.19 The Committee appreciates that ICMR has recently signed MoUs with (i) Project ECHO
(Extension of Community Healthcare Outcome), at the University of New Mexico Health Science
Centre (UNMHSC); (ii) IIT for best technology innovation; and (iii) AYUSH for traditional medicines.

14
The Committee is of the view that ICMR needs to vigorously pursue its research collaborations
and also ensure an increased emphasis on translating discoveries into health/medical products
and disseminating such discoveries in a way that is optimally beneficial to the public. The
Committee would like to be apprised of health outcomes stemming from these collaborations.
Recommendation/Observation
3.20 As per submission of the Secretary (HR), ICMR has about 800 scientists working across the 32
institutes. The Committee is of the view that for a country of the size and scale of India, the human
resource within ICMR is very small and needs to be augmented substantially. The Committee simultaneously
believes that India faces unique health challenges due to its large population and high disease burden
and augmentation of human resources of ICMR alone will not serve the purpose unless we develop a
critical mass of scientists who are dedicated to carry out basic, applied and clinical research and
innovation. It is thus obvious that enhancing the health research output will require tapping of all
available avenues of research. One of the many such avenues is the research being carried out in our
medical colleges where research is a mandate of postgraduate training in both MCI and NBE programmes.
The country produces around 30,000 Postgraduate students every year who are required to complete a
research thesis for a degree. But due to multiple reasons, like inconsequential research topics, inappropriate
research metholodies, poor guidance etc., potential scientific talent of PG students is wasted. If post-
graduate students could be guided to conduct research relevant to the national health system, critical
human resource gaps can be filled. The Committee would therefore, like the ICMR to guide post graduate
students in their dissertations by linking with them and faculty guides across India. (Para 3.7)

3.21 ICMR has a robust HRD Program and having many schemes which are meant for guidance to post
graduates students in their dissertation, MD/MS/DM/MCh/MDS thesis support. This scheme is primarily

chalk out an action plan for linking research thesis for postgraduate degree across several

ICMR Intervention with Multiple Nutrition to Fight Malnutrition
Recommendation/Observation
3.23 The Committee believes that with the intervention of multiple micro-nutrients amongst children for
eliminating malnutrition, a major problem of the country could be solved. The World Bank estimates that
India is one of the highest ranking countries in the world in respect of the number of children suffering
from malnutrition. The 2015 Global Hunger Index Report ranked India 20th amongst leading countries
with a serious hunger situation. India's National Family Health Survey (NFHS) and State Government's
School Health Programme (SHP) have also indicated that the number of anaemic and malnourished
children is rising. As per the latest SHP report for the year 2015-16, the number of anaemic children
are 6.06 lakh that increased from 5.13 lakh in 2014-15. In view of the above, the Committee recommends
that the efficacy of this intervention with multiple micro nutriments should be tested in different regions
of the country on a priority basis. If the results are successful, the intervention programme could be
implemented as a national programme to tackle malnutrition. The Committee would also like to emphasize
upon the need for co-ordination between the concerned Ministries/Departments to make the programme
successful. (Para 3.15)
Action Taken
3.24 ICMR do agree with the observations of the Committee for the problem of malnutrition in the
country and has made attempts in this direction through its National Institute of Nutrition at Hyderabad.
The Institute has come up with a micronutrient mix that is likely to be opted by Government for its
flagship programmes. The product has been tested on 400 children in Nalgonda district of Andhra
Pradesh in 2014. During initial research, scientists found that anaemia among pre-school going children
came down from 48 per cent to 10 per cent. There was an impact of micronutrient on cognitive activities
too. The micronutrient tested by the National Institute of Nutrition has seven micronutrients, including
two minerals and five vitamins. These include Vitamin A, Vitamin B12, Folic Acid and Vitamin C. An
extended multisite study is required.
Further Recommendation
3.25 The Committee is happy to note that the National Institute of Nutrition of ICMR has come
up with an effective micronutrient mix for children in management of anemia among children
during initial research in Nalgonda district of Andhra Pradesh but more multi site research
studies need to be carried out to evaluate its potential benefits. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department should conceptualize and implement the multi site research
study regarding the micronutrient within a time-frame. The Committee is, however, constrained
to note that the reply of the Department is silent on the issue of inter-Ministerial coordination
on combating anemia among children as emphasized by the Committee. The Committee, therefore,
desires to be updated in this regard.

RECOMMENDA TIONS AND OBSERV ATIONS — AT A GLANCE
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
The Committee notes from the Department's reply that year to year budgetary allocations
were decided by Ministry of Finance despite projected demand by the Department during budgetary
discussions and shortfall in allocations have affected implementation of the five newly launched
schemes in 2013-14. However, on perusal of the expenditure figures, the Committee notes that
the same are below the RE allocations made from 2012-13 to 2016-17, thereby leading to cuts
in allocations in subsequent RE allocations as a result of which the functioning of the five
schemes got adversely affected. The Committee therefore strongly recommends that in order to
ensure adequate allocations from Ministry of Finance in the future, a robust monitoring
mechanism should be put in place for proper utilisation of allocated funds through effective
financial management to ensure that the schemes do not get sidetracked due to lack of funds.
(Para 3.6)
The Committee would like to know the quantum of additional funds allocated to the
Department of Health Research at RE 2017-18 stage in pursuance to the recommendation of the
Committee. The Committee also desires to be apprised whether the Department through ICMR
generates any funds internally. (Para 3.13)
The Committee is not satisfied with the routine reply of the Department that "necessary
action will be taken to project the requirements on rational/realistic basis at RE stage". As this
is not a comprehensive reply, the Committee would like the Department to indicate the specific
action taken or proposed to be taken by it for realistic and effective budgetary formulation and
proper utilisation of allocated funds through prudent management of funds and timely
implementation of the schemes. (Para 3.16)

(Extension of Community Healthcare Outcome), at the University of New Mexico Health Science
Centre (UNMHSC); (ii) IIT for best technology innovation; and (iii) AYUSH for traditional
medicines. The Committee is of the view that ICMR needs to vigorously pursue its research
collaborations and also ensure an increased emphasis on translating discoveries into health/
medical products and disseminating such discoveries in a way that is optimally beneficial to the

collaborations. (Para 3.19)
While making the above recommendation the Committee had expected the Department to

II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendation/Observations
1.1 The Committee is constrained to note that out of the total outlay of 
` 10044.00 crores for the
Ministry for the 12th Five Year Plan, the Ministry got only ` 5186.00 crore at the BE stage. This was,
further, reduced to ` 3814.72 crores at the RE stage. Out of this, the Ministry has been able to utilize
only ` 3247.35 crores. The Committee observes the disappointing trend of utilization for the entire Five
Year Plan. The Committee in its earlier Reports on Demands for Grants has reiterated the need for the
realistic assessment of the requirement of funds and corresponding utilization of those funds. There has
been recurrent and persistent under utilization of the funds allocated at the stage of BE as well as RE
in all the five years of the 12th plan. The Committee, therefore, recommends that lessons need to be
learnt so that funds are not kept idly parked, year after year but are gainfully utilized for other fund-
starved programs / schemes. (Para 2.3)
Action Taken
1.2 The Ministry recognizes the need to fully utilize the allocated resources and in fact the steps taken
by it over the years has seen a significant improvement in this regard as per the trend of Budget allocation
vis-a-vis expenditure for the five years of the 12th Five Year Plan shown below:

PENDING UCS
Recommendation/Observations
1.4 The Committee time and again has been impressing upon the Ministry the imperative need for
speedy liquidation of pending UCs. Though some progress has been made, there is still a large number
of pending UCs and it seems that the efforts made by the Ministry to liquidate them are not enough.
The Committee, therefore, believes that a pro-active and aggressive approach is required on the part of
the Ministry for liquidation of pending UCs. The Committee is of the firm view that in this era of
e-governance and with IT resources currently available, submission of UCs should be possible almost on
"Push of a button". The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should chalk out an action
plan for online submission of UCs and also take up the matter of pendency of UCs with States which
have a large number of pending UCs like Andhra Pradesh, Bihar , Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh,
Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Uttarakhand etc. so that all pending UCs are settled within a period of six months.
(Para 2.17)
Action Taken
1.5 Presently, following remedial Action taken have been taken by the Ministry of AYUSH to reduce the
pendency of Utilization of Certificates (UCs) in respect of erstwhile Centrally Sponsored Scheme for
Development of AYUSH Hospitals & Dispensaries and National AYUSH Mission (NAM) :
(a) Various review meeting had been conducted under the Chairmanship of Secretary (AYUSH)
regarding pendency of Utilization Certificates. During the meeting of State AYUSH / Health
Ministers the issue was flagged at the level of Hon'ble MoS.
(b) The Ministry of AYUSH had nominated Nodal Officers for each State / UT to monitor the
status of pending UCs.
(c) Time to time letters have also been issued to States / UTs Government from Secretary
(AYUSH) & Joint Secretary regarding liquidation of Utilization Certificates.
(d) Regional Meeting has also been conducted under the Chairmanship of Secretary (AYUSH)
regarding various issues including liquidation of pending Utilization Certificates.
1.6 However, the recommendation of the committee including on line submission of UCs by the states
has been noted. Further, the States having large pending UCs are being specifically addressed for early
liquidation of pending UCs.
1.7 In addition, in respect of the erstwhile Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Drugs Quality Control,
States have been requested repeatedly for submission of pending UCs or refund the unspent grants. As
a result only 68 UCs worth `15.50 crore are left to be settled mainly from 6 states each having pendency
of UCs of more than ` 1 crore. In order to further ensure liquidation of UCs within a period of six
months as recommended by the Department related Parliamentary Committee; the matter has been taken
up with the concerned State Authorities for expediting submission of UCs & associated documents online
or through email.

4
IV. NATIONAL AYUSH MISSION (NAM)
Recommendation/Observations
1.8 The Committee is dismayed to note that National AYUSH Mission being one of the most important
schemes of the Ministry, would be facing shortfall of funds in Financial Year 2017-18. Similar was the
case last year i.e 2016-17 when the Secretary, Ministry of AYUSH had submitted that NAM would be
affected due to shortfall in allocation. NAM envisages better access to AYUSH services through increase
in number of AYUSH Hospitals and Dispensaries, ensuring availability of ASU&H drugs and trained
manpower , upgradation of AYUSH educational institutions for improvement in quality of AYUSH education,
increase in number of Pharmacies, setting up Drug Laboratories in States and sustained availability of
herbal raw drugs by promoting medicinal plants. Keeping in view the vital objectives of NAM, it is
imperative that adequate funds are allocated for this scheme. The Committee also is of the view that
the objectives of NAM signal a significant improvement in the quality of AYUSH healthcare services,
expanding its outreach and making available AYUSH healthcare facilities to the people. The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry should approach Ministry of Finance for additional
funds with proper justifications for enhanced allocation of funds at RE stage. (Para 4.9)
Action Taken
1.9 During 2017-18, an amount of ` 440.00 Crore has been allocated in BE. As per the recommendation
of committee Ministry of Finance will be approached for enhancement of allocation at RE stage.
V . NATIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS BOARD
Recommendation/Observations
1.10 The Committee takes note of the major findings of the study of the Indian Council of Forestry
Research and Education (ICFRE), Dehradun entailing the total commercial demand of herbal raw drugs,
exports of such drugs, consumption by domestic herbal industry as well as rural households. The
Committee believes that our country has a vast bio-diversity of medicinal plants which can be put to
great use by the Indian systems of medicine if there is proper system in place for its production,
procurement and marketing. The Committee would also like the Ministry to establish effective forward
and backward linkages to protect, sustain and encourage production of medicinal plants in a sustainable
and non-exploitative manner so that there is no distortion between demand and supply. (Para 5.6)
Action Taken
1.11 National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB) is coordinating the Medicinal Plants Component under
National AYUSH Mission (NAM) Scheme of Ministry of AYUSH for identified species of medicinal plants
including Rare, Endangered & Threatened (RET) species with the backward linkage of establishment of
nursery/seed block and forward linkages of post-harvest management like creation of infrastructure
(drying shed, storage godown), primary processing, marketing infrastructure (collection centre and retail
outlet) and uniform distribution of produce with optimum price fixation to enable good remuneration for
farmers/cultivators/collectors.

Recommendation/Observations
1.12 The Committee has been given to understand that 
` 143.00 crore has been allocated for schemes
of NER for 2017-18. Keeping in view the trend of utilization of funds for schemes of NER in

X. RESEARCH COUNCILS
Central Council for Research in Homoeopathy (CCRH)
Recommendation/Observations
1.17 The Committee observes that Homoeopathy is more popular in India than anywhere else in the
world. The Committee is, however, of the view that in order to improve the efficacy of Homoeopathy,
there is an imperative need for interdisciplinary research that focuses on correlating Homoeopathic
concepts of health and treatment with bio-medical concepts. The Committee would therefore like the
CCRH to start interdisciplinary research for exploring the scientific basis of homoeopathy concepts of
health and treatment. (Para 10.8)
Action Taken
1.18 The observations of the committee that Homoeopathy is very popular in India and many other parts
of world is very true and there is a need to undertake interdisciplinary research to enrich the scientific
base of Homoeopathy. Considering this, Council has initiated collaborative research programme to
systematically undertake interdisciplinary research projects since 2005. In this program, proposals are
invited from interested Scientists/ Institutes of repute and provided with all the technical and financial
support in a transparent manner. In fact a special committee for interdisciplinary research having eminent

7
scientists from IIT Mumbai, IIEST Kolkata, Bose institute, ICMR, AIIMS, New Delhi and many other
institutions has been constituted to give an adequate push to this research.
1.19 Studies are undertaken keeping in view the two objectives: to enrich the scientific base of homoeopathy
and to improve its application in clinical practice, development of new drugs for emerging health
challenges. Studies are aimed to understand the biological effect of homoeopathic medicines; animal
experimentation to assess anti-viral properties; physiochemical studies; standardization and optimization
of the process of drug manufacturing and to know the presence of nanoparticles in these medicines. The
focus is to elucidate the the nature of Homoeopathic medicines in physiochemical dimensions so that
standardization can be done and the theories/ concepts of homoeopathy can remain intact while applying
the modern approach to the studies. Till date Council has collaborated with various reputed institutes like
Bose Institute (Kolkata), Central Drug Research Institute (Lucknow), Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate
Medical Education and Research (JIPMER, Pondicherry), All India Institute of Medical Sciences (New
Delhi), University of Madras (Chennai), Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (Hyderabad), Panjab
University, Indian Institute of Technology (Delhi)etc. and has had 30 National and 03 International
collaborations. 33 projects have been concluded in this field and 15 are ongoing.
1.20 So far th rough these collaborations we are able to understand preventive effect of Belladonna on
Japanese Encephalitis, molecular level understanding of anti-diabetic effect of few homoeopathic
preparations, inhibitory effect of potentised medicines in kidney stone formation, mechanism of apoptotic
effect of medicines in Cancer cells by certain drugs, Lycopodium in improving the memory function,
presence of nanoparticles in Homoeopathic potencies, understanding the physicochemical nature of
Homoeopathic medicines etc.
1.21 Presently, studies for development of medicines for prevention/ treatment of Dengue, Chickungunya,
Rota virus, Acute encephalitis syndrome, Malaria, etc. are being undertaken. Studies to understand the
immune modulation in human by the homoeopathic medicines is also in progress. More studies on other
priority areas are under consideration beside this state of art of laboratories are being established at
Kolkata, and Mumbai for nurturing scientists to undertake studies in this nascent field. Ph.D. program
and fellowship scheme has been introduced this year to give impetus to interdisciplinary research.

Governments. However, the State Drug Regulatory Framework is very weak and State Drug Licensing
Authorities are ill-equipped to handle the task of regulation of AYUSH remedies. During 2016, the
Ministry has given ` 1.86 crore as grant-in-aid to the States for strengthening their quality enforcement
mechanism. The Committee observes that a large part of the population uses AYUSH remedies as
treatment of their choice. The Committee is therefore, of the opinion that the limit of financial assistance
to States needs to be increased significantly. (Para 3.5)
Action taken

merged into the National AYUSH Mission (NAM) through which 28 States have been supported in
accordance their State Action Plans for the following purposes–
(i) Strengthening of ASU&H Pharmacies of State Government/Co-operatives/Public Sector
Undertakings (PSUs).
(ii) Strengthening/establishment of State Drug Testing Laboratories.
(iii) Strengthening of ASU&H Drug Control Framework.
(iv) Engagement of technical manpower in State Drug Testing Laboratories
(v) Documentation, publication and dissemination of quality control materials.
(vi) Support for quality testing of drugs.

components including Drugs Quality Control is on the anvil. Recommendation of the PSC has been noted
and during the appraisal and analysis process of the NAM implementation, appropriate enhancement of
funding pattern and schematic guidelines may also be considered.

the public sector in the States for testing and manufacturing of ASU&H drugs. 6 States did not have

sector, there is a need to increase the number of Drug testing Laboratories and Pharmacies in the country.

III. REGULA TION AND QUALITY CONTROL OF AYURVEDIC, SIDDHA, UNANI AND
HOMOEOPATHIC (ASU&H) DRUGS
Recommendation/Observations
3.12 The Committee finds that a large number of samples of ASU&H drugs have failed the testing
procedure in 2013-14, 2014-15 and 2015-16. Even in the year 2016-17, out of 330 samples which were
tested, 36 samples have failed. Interestingly 35 samples were Homoeopathic drugs and only 1 ASU drug.
The Committee would like to point out that the Ministry has not informed about the action taken with
respect to the defaulters as done in previous years. The Committee feels that testing of samples and
consequent action thereupon is one of the most important components of quality control of ASU&H
drugs. The Committee is of the firm view that in case of samples failing the testing process, strict action
needs to be taken. However, merely issuing show cause notices, suspending/cancelling licenses would not
help as the defaulters may start with a new and different license. The Committee believes that in order
to ensure proper and effective regulation of ASU&H drugs, the defaulters must be prosecuted for trying
to play with the lives of people. The Committee, therefore, recommends that stringent measures should
be in place against the erring manufacturers so as to dissuade them from trying to pass just any
formulation as ASU&H drugs. (Para 3.7)
Action taken
3.13 The Committee is informed that as per Section 33 E, 33 EE, 33 EEA in Chapter-IV A of the Drugs
and Cosmetics Act, 1940 respectively are already in place to deal with misbranded, adulterated and
spurious ASU drugs. The State Licensing Authorities are empowered to prohibit the manufacture and sale
of ASU drugs under section 33EEC of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. Ministry of AYUSH has

27
written letters to State Government from time to time to check the quality of ASU drugs in accordance
to the provisions under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules, 1945. Nevertheless, the observations
and recommendations of Hon'ble PSC have been noted and appropriate directions tangible with the legal
provisions may be issued to the State Authorities to take effective actions against erring manufacturers.
Further Recommendation
3.14 The Committee is aware of the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules
made thereunder regarding dealing with misbranded, adulterated and spurious ASU drugs and
also about powers of State Licensing Authorities in this regard. Despite these provisions,
misbranded, adulterated and spurious ASU&H drugs have remained a festering problem and the
safety, efficacy and quality of AYUSH drugs have not been assured. The Committee would like
the Ministry to amend the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 in an appropriate manner so that
defaulters are brought to book and strict action taken against them. The Committee is of the
firm view that suitable amendments alone can help in controlling/monitoring the sale of
misbranded, adulterated and spurious ASU drugs.
Recommendation/Observations
3.15 The Committee is dismayed to note that even after two years since the decision of the creation of
a vertical structure in CDSCO was taken, no real progress has been made so far. Only 12 regulatory posts
have been notified. Recruitment rules for these posts were still in the process of finalization. The
Committee would like to point out that even through CDSCO is under the Department of Health and
Family Welfare of which the Ministry of AYUSH was once a part of, things are not moving at a swift
pace towards finalization of the vertical structure. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry
may take up this issue with the Department of Health and Family Welfare on a priority basis and also
fix a timeline for creation of this vertical structure. The Committee would like to emphasize the fact that
regulation and quality control of ASU&H drugs is one of the most important areas in the Ministry and
if the ASU&H drugs market is regulated efficiently, it will go a long way in building credibility of these
drugs and strengthen the process of mainstreaming of AYUSH. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its
recommendation made in its 95th Report that all inter-ministerial issues may be ironed out within a
designated timeline and the vertical structure created at the earliest. (Para 3.11)

amendments to the aforesaid Act, has been requested to expedite consolidation of the amendment provisions
recommended by the Task Force. But the latest submissions of the Ministry indicate that the amendment
to the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act is far from being materialized. The Committee would like the

Action Taken

Further Recommendation
3.23 The Committee is constrained to note the snail's pace of progress made in amending the
Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954. Taking into account the
fact that the lack of stringent regulatory provisions has allowed unscrupulous elements to dupe
innocent people by making tall claims about providing cure to cancer, liver cirrhosis, kidney
failure and other chronic diseases without scientific evidence, the Committee in its 75th Report
concerning Ministry of AYUSH (the then Department of AYUSH) presented to Parliament on 9th
December , 2013 had recommended that urgent measures be taken to amend the said Act. Almost
four years have passed since then, but the amendment could not be finalized. The Committee,
therefore, deprecates the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in whose legislative domain the
amendment to the said Act falls, for its inertia and indifference in the matter and would like
the Ministry of AYUSH to convey this Committee's displeasure to the former. The Committee
would also recommend that the necessary amendments be carried out expeditiously within a
specified time-frame and the outcome intimated to the Committee.
IV . NATIONAL AYUSH MISSION (NAM)
3.24 The Committee is aware that the overall standard of AYUSH education in the country continues to
be extremely poor. The Committee feels that the mandatory requirement of accreditation of teaching
hospitals and surprise inspection teams are efforts in the right direction. Further, in order to promote
AYUSH education, effective curricula reforms will also need to be carried out. The Committee also
recommends that practitioners of Allopathy should be sensitized to the strengths of AYUSH system and
to the cross system referrals between healthcare providers of all systems of medicine so that ignorance
about AYUSH is dispelled and AYUSH is integrated in the health delivery system. The Committee also
recommends that the Ministry should prepare a framework for fostering collaborative and interdisciplinary
AYUSH research of contemporary relevance. Further, NEET and NPGET test for UG and PG students
to regulate the entry of qualified students into these institutions is a much awaited step. The Committee,
therefore, recommends the Ministry that these measures may be implemented at the earliest for visible
improvement in the quality of AYUSH education. (Para 4.6)

30
Action Taken
National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) for admission in Under-Graduate course of ASU&H
colleges:
3.25 In order to bring meritorious students to the ASU&H systems of medicine in the country, a decision
was taken that the entrance exam being conducted by the private association may be stopped and all
admissions in Under-Graduate course of ASU&H colleges shall be made only through National Eligibility
cum Entrance Test (NEET) to be conducted by the CBSE from the Academic Year 2017-18. This matter
was taken up with CBSE and Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
3.26 Meanwhile, the Ministry has received representations from certain State Governments expressing
their inability to admit students into AYUSH-UG courses for the Academic Year 2017-18 as CBSE has
not included the AYUSH-UG courses in its notification. In this regard, the Ministry has also received
representations about allowing the management/NRI quota as it is being permitted for MBBS/BDS seats.
The matter was examined by the Ministry and after considering the representations made by the State
Governments, following has been decided and conveyed to the State Governments on 26.04.2017:
(i) Since, it is important to ensure that meritorious students/candidates come to AYUSH streams
of medicine, it would be advisable to the State/UT Government to adopt the merit list of NEET
for admission in AYUSH-UG courses for the Academic Year 2017-18 as per the existing
reservation policies of the concerned State Government in tune with CBSE notification of
NEET for modern medicine.
(ii) However, if due to some difficulties the State/UT Governments are unable to adopt NEET
merit list for AYUSH-UG admission for A.Y 2017-18, then such State/UT Government may
admit students in all the AYUSH Colleges/Institutions (Public and Private) through Common
Entrance Test (CET) of the concerned State Government as per the existing Rules and Policies
of the concerned State/UT/Institute/University as done in the previous year (2016-17.
(iii) Admission in AYUSH-UG Courses shall be compulsorily through NEET merit list from the A.Y .
2018-19.
Further Recommendation
3.27 The Committee appreciates the Ministry for introducing National Eligibility cum Entrance
Test (NEET) for bringing meritorious students to the AYUSH systems of medicine in the country.
The Committee would, however, like to reiterate that the Ministry must make efforts to integrate
traditional as well as modern system of medicine and education so that an integrated approach
can be taken in health delivery system. The Committee would also like to highlight the need for
curricula reforms in order to promote quality AYUSH education and recommends to the Ministry

Recommendation/Observation
3.28 It is a matter of serious concern that despite India being home to 7% of the world's bio-diversity
which makes it one of the 17 mega bio-diversity rich countries in the world, the market for medicinal

plants is not well developed in India and the country has lagged behind in maintaining the passport data
regarding place, time and phytochemical properties of medicinal plants, which are the three basic
parameters of quality assurance. Since the greatest challenge to widespread acceptance of AYUSH is
faced in quality assurance which largely depends on the source of raw materials, the Committee recommends
that the Ministry take necessary initiative to build a database that traces the source of raw materials.
(Para 5.5)

advised to take necessary initiative so that the farmers maintain passport data for medicinal plants.

to maintain passport database of medicinal plants is not enough. The Committee would, therefore,
recommend to the Ministry to play a pro-active role in this regard and incentivize the State
Governments to start maintaining a database of medicinal plants.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A GLANCE
II. BUDGET ALLOCATION
The Committee is not convinced by the achievements listed out by the Ministry with respect
to physical targets of the 12th Plan. The problem in guidelines regarding publication of Research
project paper, re-advertisement of posts, changing the nomenclature of All India Institute of
Unani Medicine, All India Institute of Homeopathy, delay in finalization of draft curriculum, non-
availability of teaching faculties, non-availability of separate psychiatry unit in NIH, Kolkata etc.
are routine issues. They could have been resolved with a streamlined monitoring mechanism for
early and timely intervention of the Ministry and necessary remedial measures taken. The
Committee also takes serious note of the fact that the Central Sector Scheme of Pharmacovigilance
of Ayurveda Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy medicines could not be implemented for want of
regulatory structure and centralized coordination system for carrying out pharmacovigilance
activities in a systematic manner. It is quite intriguing that a vertical AYUSH structure under
the aegis of the CDSCO with no specific time-frame as such is still in the process of being set
up. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to put in place a robust monitoring
mechanism with respect to the procedural issues for a better monitoring of the progress of
projects/schemes. The Committee would also like the Ministry to timely implement the scheme
of pharmacoviligance of AYUSH medicines and setting up of a vertical AYUSH structure for
quality control of AYUSH drugs and proper coordination among various AYUSH centres.
(Para 3.4)
The Committee points out that two of the fundamental issues that hamper allocation of
more funds to the Ministry are pending UCs and lack of absorption capacity. It would like to be
updated about the corrective measures taken by the Ministry to address these concerns. The
Committee also desires to be apprised of the quantum of additional funds, if any, allocated at
RE stage and utilization figures thereof. (Para 3.7)
The Committee in its previous Reports on Demands for Grants have been exhorting the
Ministry to quickly sort out the lingering issues concerning the regulatory framework of AYUSH
drugs. The Ministry has not been able to set up a central vertical structure of AYUSH drugs
regulation under CDSCO uptill now, despite the fact that the National Health Policy 2017 recognizes
the need to establish a robust and effective quality assurance mechanism for AYUSH drugs. The
feedback that Secretary (AYUSH) had taken review meeting is hardly convincing. The fact
remains that the current arrangement is not producing the intended results. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that an empowered committee may be set up to monitor the progress of
the new regulatory structure of AYUSH drugs which may submit periodical progress reports to
the Ministry. (Para 3.11)
III. REGULA TION AND QUALITY CONTROL OF AYURVEDIC, SIDDHA, UNANI AND
HOMOEOPATHIC (ASU&H) DRUGS
The Committee is aware of the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules
made thereunder regarding dealing with misbranded, adulterated and spurious ASU drugs and
37

38
also about powers of State Licensing Authorities in this regard. Despite these provisions,
misbranded, adulterated and spurious ASU&H drugs have remained a festering problem and the
safety, efficacy and quality of AYUSH drugs have not been assured. The Committee would like
the Ministry to amend the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 in an appropriate manner so that
defaulters are brought to book and strict action taken against them. The Committee is of the
firm view that suitable amendments alone can help in controlling/monitoring the sale of
misbranded, adulterated and spurious ASU drugs. (Para 3.14)
The Committee has already recommended with respect to this issue in para 3.11.
(para 3.17)
The Central Sector Scheme for developing Pharmacovigilance system for ASU&H drugs was
envisaged in the 12th Plan but the scheme could not be implemented even after conclusion of
the 12th Plan period. The Committee is of the view that this inordinate delay in implementation
of the project reflects lack of efficiency and inadequate follow-up by the administrative machinery
in the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends to the Ministry to constantly
monitor and follow up on the implementation of this important project concerning pharmacovigilance
of AYUSH drugs so that the issue of time-lag in utilization of allocated funds and implementation
of this Project is promptly addressed. (Para 3.20)
The Committee is constrained to note the snail's pace of progress made in amending the
Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954. Taking into account the
fact that the lack of stringent regulatory provisions has allowed unscrupulous elements to dupe
innocent people by making tall claims about providing cure to cancer, liver cirrhosis, kidney
failure and other chronic diseases without scientific evidence, the Committee in its 75th Report
concerning Ministry of AYUSH (the then Department of AYUSH) presented to Parliament on 9th
December, 2013 had recommended that urgent measures be taken to amend the said Act. Almost
four years have passed since then, but the amendment could not be finalized. The Committee,
therefore, deprecates the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in whose legislative domain the
amendment to the said Act falls, for its inertia and indifference in the matter and would like
the Ministry of AYUSH to convey this Committee's displeasure to the former. The Committee
would also recommend that the necessary amendments be carried out expeditiously within a
specified time-frame and the outcome intimated to the Committee. (Para 3.23)

The Committee appreciates the Ministry for introducing National Eligibility cum Entrance
Test (NEET) for bringing meritorious students to the AYUSH systems of medicine in the country.
The Committee would, however, like to reiterate that the Ministry must make efforts to integrate
traditional as well as modern system of medicine and education so that an integrated approach
can be taken in health delivery system. The Committee would also like to highlight the need for
curricula reforms in order to promote quality AYUSH education and recommends to the Ministry
to take necessary action in this regard. (Para 3.27)

REPORT
PART-A
National Health Mission (NHM)
INTRODUCTION
1.1 The National Health Mission (NHM) encompasses two sub-missions. the National Rural Health
Mission (NRHM) and the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM). The main programmatic components
include Health System Strengthening in rural and urban areas. Reproductive-Maternal-Neonatal-Child and
Adolescent Health (RMNCH+A) and Communicable and Non-Communicable Diseases. The NHM envisages
achievement of universal access to equitable. affordable and quality health care services that are accountable
and responsive to people's needs.
National Rural Health Mission (NRHM):
1.2 As per information given in the Annual Report 2017-18 of the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare. NRHM seeks to provide accessible, affordable and quality health care to the rural population.
especially the vulnerable groups. Under the NRHM. the Empowered Action Group (EAG) States as well
as North Eastern States. Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh have been given special focus.
The thrust of the Mission is to establish a fully functional. community owned. decentralized health
delivery system with inter-sectoral convergence at all levels and to ensure simultaneous action on a wide
range of determinants of health such as water, sanitation, education, nutrition, social and gender
equality.
National Urban Health Mission (NUHM):
1.3 NUHM seeks to improve the health status of the urban population particularly urban poor and other
vulnerable sections by facilitating the access to quality primary health care. NUHM covers all State
capitals, district headquarters and other cities / towns with a population of 50,000 and above (as per
Census 2011) in a phased manner. Cities and towns with population below 50,000 will continue to be
covered under NRHM.

2018-19 is less than the projected requirements however during the F.Y. 2018-19, special allocation of
`1200 crore has been allocated for Comprehensive Primary Health Care (CPHC) to be delivered through
1.5 lakh health and wellness centres. Against the projected plan outlay of ` 34882.32 crore under NHM,
funds to the tune of `30129.61 crore has been allocated for the F.Y . 2018-19. The inadequate increase

6
in outlay is likely to affect the following activities:
1. Up-scaling of existing initiatives e.g. strengthening of Health facilities to IPHS standards,
2. Establishing SHCs, PHCs and CHCs as per the norms,
3. Expansion of new vaccines of Pneumococcal Vaccine, Measles Rubella and Rota Virus to all
states.
4. Implementation of new interventions particularly those relating to Non Communicable Diseases,
5. Strengthening of District Hospitals.
2.6 The Department has further informed that the following measures have been taken to offset the
effect of shortfall of funds:
• Due to the revised Centre-State funding pattern under NHM after the 14th Finance Commission,
the total outlay for Centre and State would be ` 38,626.00 crore for the F.Y . 2018-19 with
central share of `24,908 crore. This enhanced outlay would certainly help in scaling up few
more activities under NHM.
• National Health Policy (NHP) 2017 advocates that States should raise expenditure on health
to 8% of their total Government spending. Further, as per the MoU with the State Governments,
the State Governments are required to increase health budget by 10% annually.
• The Fourteenth Finance Commission has more than doubled the grant for local bodies and
recommended that nearly all of this money should be spent on improving basic services. The
commission has fixed the grant of Rs 2.87 lakh crore which should go directly to the Gram
Panchayats and Municipalities, without any share for other levels. Under NHM, based on
proposals in Programme Implementation Plan (PIP), provision of appropriate matching support
to local bodies could be made, if the local bodies invested in strengthening healthcare delivery.
• Union Government has included cess for health and made a provision of health and education
cess which is expected to generate `11000 crore additionally.
2.7 To a question on the increase in State health budgets post the implementation of the 14th Finance
Commission, the Department in its written reply has informed that:
• Most of the States have increased their health budget during the 12th Plan. On the basis of
information made available by the States, there is a total increase of 20% in State health budget
during the 12th Plan. A statement showing the status on State Health Budget is at
Annexure-1.
• The States are required to increase their Health budget by at least 10% annually as per the
MOU with the states under the NHM. Many States have increased their health budget beyond
minimum 10% indicating more investment in health sector. The States who have failed to
increase their State health budget at BE stage generally get additional budget during the RE
stage, other-wise the 2nd tranche of release is restricted.

7

at least 10%. To provide some sort of accommodation, it is ensured that an average annual
increase of last 3 years should be at least 10%.

2.8 The Committee notes that against the against the projected outlay of ````` 34882.32 crore under
NHM (Plan), funds to the tune of `````30129.61 crore has been allocated for the F.Y. 2018-19 leaving
a shortfall of ````` 4752.71 crore. In comparison to the RE 2017-18 allocation of ````` 30786.56 crore,
the allocation for 2018-19 is abysmally less. The Committee supports the contention of the
Department that the shortfall in allocations for NHM for 2017-18 vis-a-vis its projected demand
for funds will adversely impact the following health initiatives / programmes:-
(i) Up-scaling of existing initiatives e.g. strengthening of Health facilities to IPHS standards;

to all States;

The National Health Policy (NHP) 2017 has envisaged a target of 2.5 percent of GDP as
health expenditure by the Government (Both Centre and States) by 2025. However, keeping in
view the scaling down of various activities due to reduced budgetary allocations, and the Central
share in health funding stagnating at 0.3 percent of GDP, the achievement of targets set for 2025
would remain a pipedream. The Committee is therefore of the view that the allocations provided
for 2018-19 is not in line with the pious vision set in NHP 2017 and is opposite to the vision
envisaged. The Committee therefore strongly recommends that the Department should approach
the Ministry of Finance to provide enhanced allocations for NHM in right proportion which helps
