gullible consumers who may be adults, senior citizens or children who are easily influenced and
swayed by the promises of a better quality of health and well being by consuming various food
products. Several of such advertisements may be misleading which can not only fleece the
consumers of their money for a wasted product but also harm their well being. The Committee
would like the Food Authority to take this issue with utmost seriousness and devise ways to stop
misleading advertisements. The Committee feels that FSSAI can suo-motu take cognizance of
such advertisements and involve the ASCI for appropriate actions. (Para 6.19)
The Committee recommends creation of a food advertising monitoring cell that can monitor
all the food advertisements and take up complains related to advertisements. The Committee
would like FSSAI to share information w.r.t. number of complaints received by ASCI and the
action taken against the offenders. The misleading advertisements should be banned immediately
and the information be shared with the public. (Para 6.20)
STANDARDS OF EXPORTED AND IMPORTED FOODS UNDER THE NATIONAL FOOD CONTROL
SYSTEM
The Committee recommends that whether the food is exported, imported or domestically
produced, it should follow a uniform standard and should be tested on the same parameters. The
domestic consumers cannot be treated as second class citizens and therefore the standard for
imported/ domestic production should be at par with the international benchmarks. The Committee
also recommends that there should be only one organization to overlook the National Food

116
Control System and also monitor the imported, exported and domestically manufactured food
item. (Para 6.23)
The Committee recommends that all the complaints related to food safety should be taken
seriously and immediate action should be taken by the food authority. A timeframe should be
established for speedy disposal of the cases. FSSAI should also analyse the status of pendency
in these portals. The same data should also be shared with the respective States so that immediate
action can be taken. Most of the people in the country may not be aware of the food safety
connect system and the different means through which food safety concerns can be voiced.
Therefore, the Committee recommends spreading awareness among the consumers. Skits and
Plays can be an effective method to spread awareness regarding consumer rights. A dedicated
helpline should also be opened for food safety complaints and wide scale advertisement regarding
these different means should be publicised. (Para 6.26)
The Committee recommends the creation of a cell that deals with different queries of FBOs
regarding regulations. FBOs form the backbone of the food safety regime and it is the responsibility
of the FSSAI to ensure that their problems and queries are immediately solved. Accurate
knowledge about food safety practices and procedures will help in better compliance by FBOs
which will in turn ensure production of safe food. The Committee also recommends holding
monthly meetings and seminars for the FBOs where they are provided information regarding any
change in amendments and regulations and are constantly updated with the current good
manufacturing practices. (Para 6.29)
INFORMATION EDUCATION COMMUNICATION (IEC)
The Committee applauds the FSSAI's Safe and Nutritious Food (SNF) @ School Initiative
which entails dissemination of simple food safety messages through books that have been
developed by FSSAI. The Committee reiterates the initiative of FSSAI that activities promoting
food safety should be made part of the school curriculum. More efforts have to be put to deliver
age appropriate messages to the students. The Committee recommends all the States to introduce
Yellow book developed by FSSAI in the schools. The Yellow book should also be made available
in the regional languages and necessary' changes can be made according to the region.
(Para 6.32)
The Committee recommends that FSSAI should promote computerised records rather than
insisting on registers. The digitised records will help in better data management and better
accessibility. This will also help in bringing transparency in the food business management
system and prevent unnecessary wastage of paper and loss of any information. (Para 6.34)
STANDARDS FOR LOCAL/TRADITIONAL BEVERAGES AND FOOD
The Committee recommends that FSSAI should set standards for these local beverages.
Standards for the alcoholic content in the traditional beverages will ensure the supply of quality
drinks and prevent instances of alcohol poisoning. There is a need to standardise the ingredients
use and regulate the production especially for local traditional heritage drinks so that these local
drinks are safe for consumption and at the same time commercially competitive and at par with
international drinks. (para 6.37)

117
The Committee also observes that States are famous for their local food items which are
produced by small scale industries generally in households. There is a growing demand for these
food items in other States. In view of absence of regulations for such food items, it is imperative
that to ensure safety food products of different States should adhere to basic standards of food
safety. The Committee recommends that the FSSAI should co-ordinate with State Food
Departments for monitoring of such food items generally produced by cottage small scale industries
in order to ensure adherence to basic food safety standards. (Para 6.38)
MEGA FOOD PARK
The Committee is of the view that the role of FSSAI in ensuring food safety standards in
Mega Food Parks is of immense importance as monitoring of all processes of food manufacturing
in a specified area can effectively be carried out as is being done in the Patanjali Mega Food
Park. The Committee appreciates the concept of Mega Food Park which ensures adherence to
food safety standards as well as bridging the gap between the farm and the market. The Committee
has been given to understand that all the 42 sanctioned Mega Food Parks would be operational
by 2019. In view of this, the role of FSSAI would increase and there is an urgent need for FSSAI
to augment its resources in all respects so as to carry out its mandate of an effective food quality
control management system. (Para 6.41)

3. Emphasizing the need for examining the functioning of FSSAI, the Chairman of Committee in his
opening remarks inter-alia stated that the food regulator, FSSAI is entrusted with the task of ensuring
availability of safe and wholesome food for human consumption. But despite the food regulator being
in existence, the concerns of consumers regarding safety of food products, including packaged food
products are growing. There had been a number of controversies plaguing FSSAI in the recent past.

II. Functioning of Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)
4. Thereafter, the Committee heard the Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare on the
functioning of Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. The Health Secretary threw light on the
various functions mandated to be performed by FSSAI, stating that the Food Safety and Standards
Authority of India was set up in 2008 as envisaged under Section 4 of the Food Safety and Standards
Act, 2006 and Rules and Regulations made thereunder were notified and made operational on August,
2011 with administrative authority of FSSAI being given to Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Then,
the CEO, FSSAI made a power-point presentation on the functioning of Food Safety and Standards
Authority of India. During the power-point presentation, the following points were highlighted -
(i) Integration of Food Laws across food chains like, raw material, transport, food processor, slaughter
houses, importers/wholesalers/retailers/restaurant and consumer; (ii) coverage of all kinds of food
businesses; (iii) key features of the new law and critical shifts; (iv) paradigm shifts from food adulteration
to food safety and wholesome food; (v) six key regulations were framed, namely (a) Food Safety and

123
Standards (Licensing and Registration of Food Businesses) Regulations, 2011, (b) Food Safety and
Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011, (c) Food Safety and Standards (Food Product
Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011, (d) Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and
Restriction on Sales) Regulation, 2011, (e) Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, Toxins and
Residues) Regulations, 2011, (f) Food Safety and Standards (Laboratory and Sampling Analysis) Regulations,
2011; (vi) Joint responsibility of States and Centre under the Act; (vii) Setting up of sixteen scientific
panels; (viii) Status of Standards/Regulations including horizontal standards and vertical standards;
(ix) Licensing/registration and enforcement; (x) Current status and issues of imports from different
ports; (xi) setting up of a single window clearance system from Delhi and Mumbai airports; (xii) National
network of food labs including 14 referral labs, 72 state food labs and 82 NABL accredited labs and
further action being taken/proposed; (xiii) Training and Capacity building of Food Business Operators
(FBOs); (xiv) consumer awareness e.g. joint campaign with Ministry of Consumer Affairs, like, 'Jago
Grahak Jago', etc.
5. Thereafter, members sought clarifications on (i) the role of Food Safety Commissioner in States;
(ii) status of standards/regulations; (iii) Enforcement of licensing system for all food producers; (iv) need
to ensure a national network of food labs; (v) setting up of sophisticated food labs in States; (vi) training
and capacity building of FBOs; (vii) action taken/being taken against adulteration in food/milk/water;
(viii) measures taken to curb usage of pesticides/hazardous chemicals in post harvest system in food/
vegetables; (ix) measures, if any, taken to strengthen the existing law; (x) discrepancy in reports of two
labs with regard to maggi controversy; (xi) steps taken to generate awareness among consumers
regarding expiry date of food at railway stations; (xii) steps being taken to rope in more labs and appoint
more food safety officers, etc. Some of the queries were replied to by the witnesses. The Chairman

II. Oral Evidence of Shri Vijay Sardana
4. Thereafter, the Committee heard the views of Shri Vijay Sardana, Food Safety Expert on the
functioning of FSSAI. Emphasizing on food safety, Shri Sardana was of the view that the food safety
system should be reviewed and new scientific development should be accommodated since, 80% of the
health related problems were due to bad food and water. An important issue of transparency and
accountability of the FSSAI was highlighted by him. According to him, all details from picking up of
samples; testing of samples by food testing labs and their test reports needed to be uploaded on the
website of FSSAI so that consumer is better informed and hence empowered.
5. Shri Sardana then drew attention of the Committee to the following gaps in the FSSAI Act, 2006
and made following submissions to make the Act more sound:- (i) there is no provision in FSSAI to have
surveys about consumer satisfaction/feedback and suggested to have an institutionalized mechanism for
the same; (ii) lack of transparency and proper guidelines on the process of sampling and testing of food
products; (iii) need for prompt posting of sample reports on the FSSAI website; (iv) failure of Food
Inspectors in carrying out their assigned duties and need for calling for performance reports of Food
Inspectors; (v) Indian food for export purposes, certified by Indian labs are rejected by foreign countries,
indicating failure of our testing laboratories hence, the need for making the food testing labs accountable
too; (vi) need to have a powerful analytical system for finding toxins and contaminants in food items
and laboratory strengthening measures; (vii) need to have stringent criteria for advertisement and labelling
of food products to restrict and stop misleading claims of manufacturers; (viii) FSSAI Act should be
applicable on all the e-commerce sites; (ix) need to have provisions for risk assessment and communication
wherein food companies should communicate about the risks attached to any product to the consumers
mandatorily (x) need to have a Food Alert Website for the information of consumers; (xi) need for
Central and State Food Authorities to put on their websites a monthly/bi-monthly/quarterly report on the
samples taken, samples tested and action taken on the samples found unsafe alongwith the names of
inspectors who took the sample/certifying audit party/manufacturer of the product whose articles were
found unsafe; (xii) selection and composition of the members of FSSAI based on expertise and competence
with emphasis on scientific capability especially in the appointment of CEO of FSSAI.
6. Apart from the much needed changes in the FSSAI Act, Shri Sardana was of the view that there
was a need to put in place a robust food safety management system which may include setting up food
testing centres across the country by roping in Indian Space Research Organisation/Defence Research
Development Organisation and other research institutions to develop low cost food testing lab devices
in the country itself without importing expensive laboratory machines/equipments.

which is to be adopted by FSSAI. She was of the view that vacant posts of food commissioner affect
the implementation of FSS Act in some States and mechanism of food testing at points of import should
be done. In reply to a question, she submitted that pasteurization of milk is 45% in India, and at present
the pasteurization is done at 71.5 degree celsius for 15 seconds which is effective in killing all micro-
organisms including tuberculosis bacteria making pasteurized milk TB free.
8. Thereafter, Dr. B. Dinesh Kumar, Scientist F, National Institute of Nutrition during his deposition
inter-alia highlighted that there is need to establish more accredited labs and strengthen the existing labs
for food testing, symbol based food labelling should be made for easy understanding, efforts should be
made to enhance the food safety and food label reading skills among the children by making them part
of skill building activity in schools, fortification of certain foods like vegetable oils, milk etc. for the
purpose of reducing malnutrition. It was also suggested that FSSAI should work towards creating 'food
advertising monitoring cell' to take up false and misleading advertisements to the appropriate authorities
and 'Food Risk Communication Wing' which would serve as one stop shop for authentic and verified
scientific information of all food items.
9. The Committee, then, heard the views of Shri S.M. Bhardwaj, President. Food Analysts Association
(India) who inter-alia highlighted various issues viz. no defined status of food analyst in FSSA and rules
made thereunder, paucity of technical manpower, no engagement of FSSAI in policy making, no direct
recruitment of officers for key posts. It was suggested that FSS Act must be re-written to make it
relevant for the country, enforcement staff must be given place in constituting authority under section
5, 11 and 14 of FSS Act, way to dispose off seized items should be delineated in the Act, etc.

133
10. Thereafter, Shri Amit Prakash Verma, Food Safety Officer Cadre Association highlighted the
inadequacies in the present FSS Act 2006 viz. lack of clarity regarding procedure of disposal of seizures,
and process to keep the seized articles in custody of FBOs, non cooperation of FBOs with regulatory
authority, non inclusion of Drinking/portable water in definition of water in the Act. He also stated that
the appointment of officer from a non science background hampers the functioning of food safety.
11. Shri Sudhir Kumar Desai, Member, The Solvent Extractors' Association of India, Mumbai inter alia
highlighted the following points viz. removal of mandatory AGMARK certification, doing away with
storage control order, banning of sale of loose oil, fortification of oils by Vitamin A, D on voluntary basis
and crude/virgin/raw oils should be kept out of the purview of fortification, etc.
12. Thereafter, Shri Pradip Chakraborty , Former Director, FSSAI inter alia highlighted various issues
infringing on the functioning of FSSAI like lack of infrastructure in States, non technical food officers,
ineffective enforcement of FSS Act, etc. He suggested that regulations need to change and packaging
and labelling should be harmonized with CODEX etc. The Committee also directed that the recommendations
of the Codex Alimentarious Commission for the quality and safety of food be called for from the Ministry
of Health and Family Welfare.
13. During the course of the meeting, Members raised certain queries on the said subject. The witnesses
replied to some of the queries raised by the Members. The Chairman directed the witnesses to furnish
detailed written replies to the queries left unanswered within a week.
14. A verbatim record of the proceedings of the meeting was kept.

II. Oral evidence of the Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare along with the
officials of the FSSAI on the functioning of FSSAI
4. The Committee heard the views of Secretary of Department of Health and Family Welfare on the
functioning of FSSAI and the Secretary gave a brief outline regarding the subject. Thereafter CEO of
FSSAI made a power point presentation on the subject and inter alia  highlighted the following points
like—
(i) development of FSSAI and paradigm shifts from fragmented approach to a single food law,
from combating adulteration in food product to food safety across food chain, from prosecution
to prevention and capacity building to build a culture of self compliance;
(ii) ensuring safe and wholesome food through its four pillars namely (a) food standards and safe
practices, (b) food testing, (c) food safety compliance and (d) training and capacity building;
(iii) development of Quick Access System which is a one point source for all vertical and horizontal
Food Standards and Lab Management System;
(iv) Food Safety Knowledge Assimilation Network for development of science based standards;
(v) harmonisation with globally benchmarked standards (Codex);
***Relate to other matters.

136
(vi) status of notified Labs and support for State Food Labs;
(vii) introduction of new testing methods and Indian Food Laboratory Network;
(viii) introduction of food safety on wheels and Mobile Testing Labs to strengthen the food testing
infrastructure in the States;
(ix) strengthening of the process of licensing, registration, enforcement of FSSAI rules and
regulations;
(x) domestic food control through smart and digital compliance;
(xi) food import control at 20 ports;
(xii) training and capacity building programme for the food safety supervisors, food testing and
regulatory staff;
(xiii) setting up of food fortification standards to address the micronutrients deficiency;
(xiv) focus on elimination of trans-fats by 2022;
(xv) proper food labelling to reduce intake of high fat, sugar and salt foods in order to prevent non-
communicable diseases;
(xvi) launch of various books to bring about social and behavioural changes and increase consumer
awareness;
(xvii) development of mobile apps for consumer and a dedicated food smart consumers portal.
5. He further deliberated upon the challenges faced by FSSAI - (a) shortage of regulatory staff,
(b) poor food testing infrastructure, (c) training and capacity building issues, (d) lacunae in Food Safety
and Standards Act, Rules and Regulation.
